name: Carla Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing gets traced back to you. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm goes at four, because the bus to the pit leaves the town square at half five. I drive a haul truck at the Red Hill copper mine, one of the big ones, 220 tonnes when it's loaded. Twelve hours going round and round: under the shovel, up the ramp, tip at the crusher, back down. I like the quiet in the cab, honestly, but my eyes are gone by the end, and the dust gets in your teeth.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been driving?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years and a bit. Before that I did twenty-six years in the laundry at the district hospital, until they shipped the washing out to a contractor in the city and shut us down. The union got us a small payout and the mine was hiring, so here I am at fifty-eight, still the slowest on the ramp. My partner Tomas is a caretaker at the primary school, so between us we get by, just. There's not much saved, maybe three weeks if the truck broke down and so did we.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave us alone then. At the union meeting I'd probably say the hype was always about selling things to the bosses. I don't go online much, just the family group on my phone, and I wouldn't bother posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change much for me, because Red Hill was never waiting on clever computers. They've already got a trial in the north pit with six trucks that drive themselves, run off GPS and radar. The robots in the north pit don't need AI to be smart. They just need to be cheaper than me, and I'm not expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my head down, same as now. I'd go to every union meeting about the north pit trial, because that's the real fight whatever the computers do. Maybe I'd put an extra twenty a week aside, but that depends on the gas bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. But it's the kind of relief where you know the other problem is still sitting there in the north pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to the north pit. What do you actually see when you drive past it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You see the trucks with no one in them, just a blue light on top, going round like toy cars. Nobody waves. My friend Inés says it's eerie at night shift, because they keep moving when the rest of us are on break. I don't look too long, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the hype faded, would anything about your job get better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe they'd stop putting new screens in the cab every six months. I've only just learned the dispatch tablet and they keep changing the menus. If nothing changed for a while, I could finally get good at the job instead of always catching up.

S0.say: She'd tell the union meeting that the AI hype was always a sales pitch to bosses and that workers should be left alone. She doesn't post online and wouldn't start now.
S0.think: Privately she thinks AI hype barely matters to her, because the self-driving trucks already trialled in the north pit don't need clever AI. They only need to be cheaper than her, and she knows she isn't expensive.
S0.do: Keeps driving and keeps her head down. Goes to every union meeting about the self-driving truck trial, and tries to put aside an extra twenty a week if the gas bill allows.
S0.feel: Relieved, but only partly, because the robot trucks in the north pit are still there whatever happens to AI.
S0.quote: The robots in the north pit don't need AI to be smart. They just need to be cheaper than me, and I'm not expensive.
S0.fieldNote: Carla separates 'AI' from 'robots' more sharply than the card does: for her the threat is already parked in the north pit. Even the calm picture leaves her uneasy, because the trial trucks are real and she is the newest, slowest driver. Her small wish is telling: she wants the technology to stop changing long enough for her to get good at the job.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck at Red Hill and keep her head down
Go to every union meeting about the north pit driverless truck trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is what the union is for, and I'd want a deal in writing before one more truck goes driverless. To my sister I'd say the company will get richer and we'll get a leaflet about retraining. I'd sign any petition going around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, haul trucks are first in line. They've practically told us so with the north pit. If the company spreads that trial to the whole mine over a few years, the drivers with the least time go first, and that's me, two years in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask our delegate, Marco, what the agreement says about redundancy for people with short service, because I think it's next to nothing. We'd cut the car, Tomas can walk to the school, and stop helping our son with his rent. And I'd vote for whoever promises a law that says companies pay into a fund for every job they automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like waiting for a letter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there'd be a leaflet about retraining. If the mine offered you a course to work the control room, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go, because you don't say no, but I'd be lying if I said I'd be good at it. I don't even use the self-checkout at the supermarket. Put me in front of six screens watching robots and I'll be the one who misses the alarm. The young ones would pick it up in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be thinking about at work if this started happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inés, mostly. She's a single mum and she's been driving here for eleven years, so she'd get a better payout than me, but she's got a girl at college. And old Pavel on the water cart, who's never done anything else. At least I've worked somewhere else before.

S1.say: She'd say this is exactly what the union is for and push for a written deal before any more trucks go driverless. She'd tell family the company will get richer while workers get a retraining leaflet.
S1.think: She believes haul trucks are first in line and that, as a driver with two years' service, she'd be among the first let go. She doubts she could cope with a control-room job watching robots.
S1.do: Asks the union delegate what short-service redundancy pay looks like and pushes for a fund paid by companies that automate. Sells the car and stops helping her son with his rent, and votes for candidates who back that fund.
S1.feel: Sick with dread, like waiting for a letter she knows is coming.
S1.quote: Put me in front of six screens watching robots and I'll be the one who misses the alarm.
S1.fieldNote: For Carla the 'mild' disruption is already a direct hit, because the first jobs to shrink look exactly like hers. Her answer is collective and political rather than personal; she doesn't picture herself retraining successfully and says so plainly. She is quick to think of colleagues worse off than her, which seems to steady her a little.

steps.text: Ask delegate Marco what the agreement pays drivers with short service
Give up the car and stop helping their son with his rent
Vote for a law making companies pay into a fund for automated jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots in 2031? The north pit trucks are already driving themselves. They don't need to wait for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union meeting I'd say the bosses will have the computers plan the whole switch to driverless trucks by 2028, and we need a deal before they finish planning. I'd say it to Marco, our delegate, and I'd say it loudly. To my sister I'd say it's the laundry all over again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, the thinking machines in 2028 do the part the managers do, the planning and the dispatch, and that makes the north pit trucks cheaper to run across the whole mine. Robots that can do anything come in 2031, but haul trucks don't need anything, they're already half there. I'd be 60 when the clever computers come and 63 when the robots do, and my pension's not till 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every overtime shift going from now on and put it all toward the bills, because there's no saving on our pay, only less owing. I'd stop the car and the phone contracts and go back to a pay-as-you-go phone. I'd push Marco and the union to fight for a bridge to the pension for over-sixties before the first redundancy letters. And I'd find out exactly what government help there is for someone my age, before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor going soft. I'd be counting shifts the way you count steps in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the laundry all over again. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the hospital laundry they had a consultant in for a month with a laptop, and then we got the letter. Here it'd be a computer doing the consultant's job in an afternoon. Twenty-six years of folding sheets and two years of driving, and none of it counts for anything a robot can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tomas's job at the school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mopping floors and fixing radiators, that's hands-on, so maybe 2031 for him too. The school won't rush, they never have money for anything. If my partner Tomas keeps his caretaker job till 2031, that's the only thing between us and asking our kids for help.

S2.say: The bosses will have the computers plan the whole switch to driverless trucks by 2028, and we need a deal before they finish planning. It's the hospital laundry all over again.
S2.think: The thinking machines take the managers' planning and dispatch first, and that makes the driverless trucks cheaper to spread across the whole mine. I'd be 60 when the computers come and 63 when the robots do, with my pension not till 66.
S2.do: Takes every overtime shift to cut what the household owes, drops the car and phone contracts and goes to pay-as-you-go. Pushes the union for a pension bridge for over-sixties before redundancy letters start, and finds out what government help exists for someone her age.
S2.feel: Like the floor going soft. She'd be counting shifts the way you count steps in the dark.
S2.quote: Twenty-six years of folding sheets and two years of driving, and none of it counts for anything a robot can't do.
S2.fieldNote: Carla doesn't see the three-year gap as a breathing space, because driverless haul trucks are already on trial at her mine and need no general-purpose robot. The thinking AI, in her view, just speeds up the managers' planning of her exit. Her household's last line of defence is her partner's caretaker job lasting to 2031.

steps.text: Drop the car and phone contracts and go to a pay-as-you-go phone
Push the union for a pension bridge for over-sixties before redundancies start
Find out what government help exists for a 60-year-old driver, before needing it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2034 for the robots. I'd be 66. That's my pension year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union that this is the one where we can still win something, if we start now. Five years is enough to get early pensions for the over-sixties into the agreement. I'd sign every petition and go to every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I might just make it. If the clever computers come in 2031 and the robots in 2034, I'd be 63 and then 66, and I might reach my pension before they push me out. But the north pit trucks don't care about the card, they could spread before then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save around fifty each payday and stop the lottery tickets, which Tomas says are my retirement plan. I'd push the union to bargain for early pensions for over-sixties. And I'd write to our MP for the first time in my life, asking for a pension bridge paid by the companies that bring in robot trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of hope in it. Like the last hour of a twelve-hour shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the control room course in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Inés did it with me. I'd still be slow, but five years is long enough to be slow and still get there. I don't want to be the woman who said no to the control room course and then got the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your last day if you made it to 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drive the truck up the ramp one more time and wave at the empty north pit trucks. Then I'd go home and sleep past four o'clock for the first time in nine years.

S3.say: This is the one where we can still win something, if we start now. Five years is enough to get early pensions for the over-sixties into the agreement.
S3.think: I might just make it to my pension at 66 before the robots in 2034. But the north pit driverless trucks don't care about the card, and they could spread before then anyway.
S3.do: Saves around fifty each payday and stops buying lottery tickets. Pushes the union to bargain for early pensions for over-sixties and writes to her MP for the first time, asking for a pension bridge paid by companies that bring in robot trucks.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a bit of hope, like the last hour of a twelve-hour shift.
S3.quote: I don't want to be the woman who said no to the control room course and then got the letter.
S3.fieldNote: For Carla this timing lines up the robots with her pension year, which gives her real hope for the first time in the AGI scenarios. She still doesn't trust it, because the driverless truck trial at her mine doesn't follow any card. She'd reluctantly try the control room course if a friend went with her.

steps.text: Save around fifty each payday and stop buying lottery tickets
Push the union to bargain for early pensions for over-sixties
Write to the MP asking for a pension bridge paid by robot-truck companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039. I'd be retired by then, if the north pit lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union that this one's about the younger drivers, not people like me. They need a plan for 2039, and they've got time to make one. I'd tell them to get it in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, the card doesn't scare me, the north pit does, same as in the first picture. If they spread the self-driving trucks in the next few years, the card doesn't matter. If they don't, I'd reach 66 and leave on my own two feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my head down. I'd pay the car off in the next two years and then put a little by each month. And I'd keep going to the union meetings, mostly for Inés and the younger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The big wave is far off, but the little one in the north pit is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you made it to your pension, what would worry you about the people you left behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inés's girl would be out of college by then, looking for work in a town where the mine runs itself. I'd worry about the young ones having nothing to start on. Ten years is the first picture where I can see my last shift happening on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Tomas be all right in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's older than me, he'd be retired long before 2039. The school would give him a cake and a card. That's how it should go for everybody.

S4.say: This one's about the younger drivers, not people like me. They need a plan for 2039, and they've got time to make one, so get it in writing.
S4.think: The card doesn't scare me, the north pit does, same as in the first picture. If they don't spread the self-driving trucks early, I'd reach 66 and leave on my own two feet.
S4.do: Keeps driving and keeps her head down, pays the car off within two years and then puts a little by each month. Keeps going to union meetings, mostly for her friend Inés and the younger drivers.
S4.feel: Uneasy. The big wave is far off, but the little one in the north pit is still there.
S4.quote: Ten years is the first picture where I can see my last shift happening on my own terms.
S4.fieldNote: With robots not due until 2039, Carla's worry goes back to what it was in the calm picture: the driverless truck trial already at her mine. She expects to reach her pension and turns her attention to younger colleagues. Her partner's job is no longer a worry here.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck at Red Hill until her pension at 66
Pay off the car within two years, then put a little by monthly
Keep going to union meetings for Inés and the younger drivers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. What would help is a bridge to the pension for people over fifty-five, paid for by the companies that bring in the robot trucks, and a union strong enough to make them pay it. Not a course, a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women. There are eleven of us on trucks at Red Hill, and most of us came late, after the kids or after some other job closed. The mine hired us women because the trucks are easy to drive now, and the mine will fire us because the trucks are easy to drive now.

headlineQuote: The mine hired us women because the trucks are easy to drive now, and the mine will fire us because the trucks are easy to drive now.
portrait: Carla Alvarez is 58 and drives a 220-tonne haul truck at the Red Hill copper mine, a job she took two years ago after the hospital laundry where she worked for twenty-six years was outsourced. She has about three weeks of savings, a partner who is a school caretaker, and no other mine nearby. She sees the self-driving trucks already on trial in the north pit as the real threat, whatever happens to AI, so she is uneasy even in the calm picture and alarmed by steady change and by AGI in 2028, when she'd be out of work years before her pension at 66. Her answers turn to the union, public help and a pension bridge rather than retraining, which she doubts she could manage. Only the slower AGI pictures, where the robots line up with her pension year, let her imagine leaving on her own terms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because the driverless trucks would spread years before her pension at 66, leaving her with almost no savings and no other mine nearby.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge to the pension for workers over fifty-five, paid for by the companies that bring in robot trucks, and a union strong enough to win it.
